analysis.one_liner: Restores the estate tax on fortunes over $3.5 million, raises top rates, and closes trust loopholes.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a hearing or vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, with a single Democratic cosponsor, and never came out before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would reinstate a stronger estate tax: estates worth more than $3.5 million would owe tax, with rates climbing to 55% for estates over $50 million and a 10% surtax on the portion of estates over $500 million. It would also close common ways the wealthiest families shrink or avoid the tax — short-term trusts, "grantor" trusts, deep valuation discounts, and century-long "dynasty" trusts — while doubling the special valuation break for family farmland and enlarging the break for donating conservation easements. It never received any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal Treasury and the general public, through added revenue paid only by the largest inheritances; family farms, which would get a $3 million inflation-adjusted farmland valuation break; and land conservation, since the deduction for donating conservation easements would rise to $2 million at a 60% rate. Families passing on less than $3.5 million would owe no estate tax at all.
analysis.who_benefits_short: General public, family farms, conservation donors

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the estate tax exemption to $3.5 million per person and raises rates so estates over $50 million pay up to 55%, with a 10% surtax on everything above $500 million — so only the largest inheritances pay more.

Triples the special farmland valuation reduction to $3 million and adjusts it for inflation, shielding family farms and businesses from estate tax pressure when a farm's value reflects land prices rather than income.
Raises the estate tax exclusion for donated conservation easements to $2 million and increases the excluded share to 60%, rewarding families that permanently protect land.

Closes the main planning loopholes the very wealthy use: heirs could no longer report a lower value to the IRS than the estate reported (consistent-basis reporting), short 2-year GRATs would need a 10-year minimum term, grantor trusts would be subject to transfer tax, family valuation discounts would be limited, and trusts would lose the generation-skipping exemption if they can last longer than 50 years.

analysis.who_pays: Heirs of estates worth more than $3.5 million — especially families with over $50 million (55% rate) and over $500 million (surtax) — plus wealthy users of GRATs, grantor trusts, valuation discounts, and dynasty trusts, and the estate-planning professionals who sell those services. Executors and donors would also face new reporting duties and penalties for inconsistent values.

drawbacks.text: New paperwork: executors and gift donors would have to report the value of every interest to the Treasury and to each recipient, with penalties for values that don't match the estate or gift return — real added cost and complexity for estate administration.

The anti-abuse rules sweep in legitimate planning too: a mandatory 10-year minimum GRAT term, limits on valuation discounts for family business interests, and caps on the annual gift exclusion for transfers in trust or of illiquid interests could complicate ordinary succession of a family business, not just avoidance by the rich.

Opponents argue the estate tax amounts to taxing wealth a second time after it was already subject to income and capital-gains tax; the bill raises that tax rather than addressing the underlying capital-gains treatment, and its provisions apply to deaths and transfers after December 31, 2015, leaving little transition time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on the largest estates and the trust-planning industry, while the bill specifically sweetens the rules for family farms and conservation donors — the groups most often cited against estate tax increases. The main honest cost is compliance: new disclosure duties and tighter valuation rules add administrative burden for executors, donors, and small family businesses, and the transition was abrupt (effective for deaths after 2015). On balance the design is well targeted, but it was a tax increase aimed at a concentrated group, which is exactly why it had no path in the committee it was sent to.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it simply expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on June 25, 2015; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance that same day.
It drew exactly one cosponsor, a Senate Democrat, and no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote appears in the action history for the rest of the 114th Congress.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill died in committee, as most bills referred to committee without leadership backing do.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Heirs to the largest estates and wealthy families using GRATs, grantor trusts, valuation discounts, and long-horizon dynasty trusts kept the lower exemption, the 40% top rate, and the planning tools the bill would have curtailed — along with the estate-planning industry that serves them.

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case for taxing the largest estates and closing trust loopholes.

for.name: 1 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican supported the bill and the Senate never considered it; the majority's agenda did not include raising the estate tax.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only sponsors were an independent who caucuses with Democrats and one of 44 Senate Democrats, while the Republican-chaired Finance Committee took no action and no Republican backed it.

industries.note: The bill's core provisions target the industry's most profitable products — short-term GRATs, grantor trust sales, family valuation discounts, and long-dated dynasty trusts. Its death preserved that business intact.
Estates over $3.5 million would have paid more, with a 55% rate above $50 million and a 10% surtax above $500 million. Because the bill died, no estate paid the higher rates.
The bill triples the special farmland valuation reduction to $3 million and indexes it to inflation, easing estate tax pressure on heirs of farm land.
Larger estate tax exclusion ($2 million at 60%) for donated conservation easements gives landowners a bigger incentive to permanently protect land.
